**Started 2026-10-21. No claim on this page has been checked against its
source.** Every entry is ❌. The one-line description on each comes from an
abstract or a search result. Bibliographic details for entries carrying a
link were confirmed by search on 2026-10-21; entries marked *citation not
confirmed* are written from memory and need their details checked before they
are cited anywhere else.
:::

This page is the reference list behind the
[working specification](specification.qmd), and uses its thirteen kinds of
validation and their numbers. Under each kind it lists what already exists.
Pharmacometrics (PMX) is covered in depth. Software engineering is covered at
the level of ideas to borrow. Medical devices, health
economics, clinical prediction models and Bayesian statistics each have
frameworks that PMX can learn from, and they get their own section.

**Out of scope:** evaluating an AI model in general, such as benchmarks;
computerized system validation in the regulatory sense, such as 21 CFR Part
11; and the laboratory side of assay validation beyond what a modeler needs
to know to trust the numbers.

## Status Markers

- ❌ **Not checked.** No claim drawn from this source has been verified
  against it.
- ⚠️ **Transcribed, unverified.** A number or a structure on this page came
  from the source and has not been checked against it.
- ✅ **Checked.** The description on this page has been verified against the
  source.

Change a marker when the check is done, not when the paper is opened.

## Where to Start

Seven sources, in reading order. The first three set the frame; the rest
cover the kinds most often done badly.

1. **ICH M15 (2026).** The harmonized framework for planning and assessing
   model-informed drug development (MIDD) evidence, from question of interest
   to model risk. It is the vocabulary regulators will now use.
2. **Marshall et al. 2016, the MID3 good practices paper.** The industry
   consensus on how MIDD work is planned, done and documented.
3. **Musuamba et al. 2021.** How EMA regulators judge the credibility of a
   mechanistic model, with a credibility matrix applied to three cases.
4. **Nguyen et al. 2017.** The ISoP tutorial on model diagnostics for
   continuous data, with each plot shown for a correct and a misspecified
   model.
5. **Bonate et al. 2012.** The one PMX paper on quality control of the data,
   control streams and outputs, which is where checking the code and the
   dataset is written down.
6. **Overgaard et al. 2015**, read with **Dai et al. 2020.** Good practice for
   exposure-response analysis, and the confounding that makes it hard for
   monoclonal antibodies.
7. **FDA draft guidance on AI for regulatory decision-making (2025).** A
   seven-step credibility framework for AI models, the nearest thing to
   guidance on validating work an AI produced.

## The Taxonomy

Thirteen kinds, grouped by what is being asked about. Validation and
verification are used here in the engineering sense that ASME V&V 40 and the
ISPOR-SMDM task force share: **verification** asks whether something was
built right, and **validation** asks whether it is the right thing.

| # | Kind | Asks | V or V |
|---|---|---|---|
| | **The question and the study** | | |
| 1 | Question | Is this the right question for the decision? | Validation |
| 2 | Study design | Can this nonclinical or clinical study answer the question? | Validation |
| 3 | Causal assumptions | Could a confounder explain the relationship? | Validation |
| | **The data** | | |
| 4 | Assay | Does the assay measure what the model assumes, accurately enough? | Both |
| 5 | Analysis dataset | Was the dataset built correctly from the right sources? | Verification |
| 6 | Sources and prior knowledge | Does each claim and prior say what its source says? | Verification |
| | **The analysis** | | |
| 7 | Code | Do the model, plotting and simulation code compute what they claim? | Verification |
| 8 | Model | Does the model describe the data, with plausible parameters? | Validation |
| 9 | Predictions | Is the uncertainty stated, and does the model predict better than a simple one? | Validation |
| | **The claims** | | |
| 10 | Conclusions | Does the conclusion follow from the result? | Validation |
| 11 | Communication | Do the figures and report show what was found, without overstating it? | Validation |
| | **Afterwards** | | |
| 12 | Reproducibility | Can someone else rerun it and get the same numbers? | Verification |
| 13 | Use | Was the answer used for the decision it was meant for? | Validation |

: Thirteen kinds of validation {tbl-colwidths="[4,20,60,16]"}

A framework that spans all thirteen comes first, then one section per kind,
each with the same three parts: what the kind asks, what exists, and the gap.

## Credibility Frameworks That Span Every Kind

These set how much validation an activity needs from the risk of the
decision it informs. The move is the same in all of them: name the question
and the context of use, judge how much the decision rests on the model and
what a wrong answer costs, and scale the evidence to that.

- ❌ **ICH M15, General principles for model-informed drug development.**
  Step 4 on 29 January 2026; FDA guidance June 2026; in effect in the EU from
  23 July 2026. Six elements: question of interest, context of use, model
  influence, consequence of a wrong decision, model risk and model impact.
  [EMA copy](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-m15-guideline-general-principles-model-informed-drug-development-step-5_en.pdf).
- ❌ **ASME V&V 40-2018**, Assessing credibility of computational modeling
  through verification and validation: application to medical devices. The
  origin of the risk-informed credibility framework the drug guidances
  borrowed.
- ❌ **Kuemmel et al. 2020**, Consideration of a credibility assessment
  framework in model-informed drug development: potential application to
  physiologically-based pharmacokinetic modeling and simulation. *CPT:
  Pharmacometrics & Systems Pharmacology* 9:21–28.
  [doi:10.1002/psp4.12479](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12479). The FDA paper
  that carried V&V 40 into drug development. It is the source of the
  [Context of Use table](../../references/ContextOfUse_Table_1page.pdf).
- ❌ **Musuamba et al. 2021**, Scientific and regulatory evaluation of
  mechanistic in silico drug and disease models in drug development: building
  model credibility. *CPT: PSP* 10:804–825.
  [PMC8376137](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8376137/). EMA
  Modelling and Simulation Working Party authors; a credibility matrix tried
  on three cases.
- ❌ **Marshall et al. 2016**, Good practices in model-informed drug discovery
  and development: practice, application, and documentation. *CPT: PSP*
  5:93–122. [doi:10.1002/psp4.12049](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12049). The
  EFPIA MID3 workgroup's white paper. A 2019 follow-up by Marshall et al.
  surveyed industry, FDA and EMA staff on how well it matches practice.
- ❌ **Erdemir et al. 2020**, Credible practice of modeling and simulation in
  healthcare: ten rules from a multidisciplinary perspective. *J Transl Med*
  18:369. [PMC7526418](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7526418/).
  From the NIH Interagency Modeling and Analysis Group's committee; argues
  that verification and validation alone are not credible practice.
- ❌ **FDA draft guidance, January 2025**, Considerations for the use of
  artificial intelligence to support regulatory decision-making for drug and
  biological products.
  [FDA page](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/considerations-use-artificial-intelligence-support-regulatory-decision-making-drug-and-biological).
  Seven steps: question of interest, context of use, model risk, credibility
  plan, execution, documentation, adequacy. Still a draft when last searched.
  It is written for an AI model that produces evidence, not for an AI agent
  doing the analyst's work, which is the case this project cares about.
- ❌ **EMA reflection paper on the use of artificial intelligence in the
  medicinal product lifecycle** (2024). *Citation not confirmed.*

**Gap.** All of these scale the depth of evidence to the risk. None says
which checks to run inside an analysis, which is what the sections below
collect.

## 1. Question

**Asks.** Is this the right question for the decision, with a named person
who will use the answer, and is the analysis sized to it?

- ❌ [Context of Use table](../../references/ContextOfUse_Table_1page.pdf),
  adapted from Kuemmel et al. 2020.
- ❌ [Dose Finding Framework](https://ascpt.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/psp4.12701),
  *CPT: PSP*.
- ❌ ICH M15, the question of interest and context of use (above).
- ❌ Gadkar et al. 2016 (under 8, Model), whose first two stages are project
  needs and scope.

**Gap.** Everything here is used before the work. Nothing checks at the end
that the answer still answers the question asked at the start.

## 2. Study Design

**Asks.** Can the nonclinical or clinical study answer the question the
analysis will put to it? For a model this means: are the doses spread widely
enough to estimate a dose-response, are samples taken when the drug and the
response are changing, are there enough subjects, and is the population the
one the prediction is for?

**Clinical study design.**

- ❌ **ICH E8(R1)**, General considerations for clinical studies (2021),
  which introduced quality by design and critical-to-quality factors.
  *Citation not confirmed.*
- ❌ **ICH E9** and **E9(R1)**, statistical principles for clinical trials
  and the estimand framework (addendum 2019). E9(R1) asks what quantity a
  trial is meant to estimate, which is the same question as the context of
  use. *Citation not confirmed.*
- ❌ **SPIRIT statement**, the checklist for clinical trial protocols (2013,
  updated 2025). *Citation not confirmed.*
- ❌ **FDA guidance, August 2024**, Optimizing the dosage of human prescription
  drugs and biological products for the treatment of oncologic diseases
  (Project Optimus).
  [FDA page](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/optimizing-dosage-human-prescription-drugs-and-biological-products-treatment-oncologic-diseases).
  Expects randomized comparison of more than one dose before registration.
- ❌ **FDA guidance, April 2003**, Exposure-response relationships: study
  design, data analysis, and regulatory applications.
  [PDF](https://fda.gov/media/71277/download). Has a chapter on designing
  a study so that exposure-response can be estimated. No revision was found.
- ❌ **EMA guideline, 2017**, Strategies to identify and mitigate risks for
  first-in-human and early clinical trials with investigational medicinal
  products (EMEA/CHMP/SWP/28367/07 Rev. 1). Starting dose, escalation,
  maximum dose and stopping rules.
  [EMA news item](https://www.ema.europa.eu/el/news/revised-guideline-first-human-clinical-trials).

**Nonclinical study design.**

- ❌ **Percie du Sert et al. 2020**, The ARRIVE guidelines 2.0: updated
  guidelines for reporting animal research. *PLoS Biol* 18:e3000410.
  [PMC7360023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7360023). The
  "Essential 10" covers randomization, blinding and sample size, which decide
  whether an animal PK/PD study can be modeled at all.
- ❌ **ICH M3(R2)**, **S6(R1)** and **S9**, the nonclinical safety guidelines
  for small molecules, biotechnology products and anticancer drugs, which set
  what nonclinical studies exist to model. *Citation not confirmed.*

**Design for modeling.**

- ❌ **Nyberg et al. 2012**, PopED, the optimal design tool for nonlinear
  mixed-effects models. *Comput Methods Programs Biomed*.
  [doi:10.1016/j.cmpb.2012.05.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmpb.2012.05.005).
  [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=PopED). Computes how well a
  proposed design would estimate the model's parameters before the study runs.
- ❌ **Holford et al. 2000**, Simulation of clinical trials. *Annu Rev
  Pharmacol Toxicol* 40:209–234. *Citation not confirmed beyond a search
  listing.*
- ❌ This site's [Sizing Studies](../pmx-sizing-studies/index.qmd) project.

**Gap.** The design literature optimizes a study or reports it. No PMX
checklist asks, before an analysis starts, whether an existing study can
support the model the analysis intends to fit: whether the dose range,
sampling and sample size are enough for the parameters the decision rests on.
PopED answers that quantitatively for a planned design, and is rarely run
backwards on a study already done.

## 3. Causal Assumptions

**Asks.** What causes what in the system, and could a variable that affects
both exposure and response explain the relationship the model estimates?

- ❌ Causality Checklist and Guidance for PMX:
  [PDF](../../files/causality-checklist.pdf) ·
  [Google Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Hc3RoTJXS-PQCUm-rG_RCuEa3ykRj5FiAtqRwgSiX6M/edit).
- ❌ [Causal diagrams for understanding when correlation doesn't imply causation](../../files/2021-10-12-causal-diagrams.pdf),
  a 2021 talk.
- ❌ **Rogers, Maas and Pérez Pitarch 2023**, An introduction to causal
  inference for pharmacometricians. *CPT: PSP* 12:27–40.
  [doi:10.1002/psp4.12894](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12894). Potential
  outcomes, the g-formula and directed acyclic graphs, with an example of
  correlated covariates in a population PK model.
- ❌ **Dai, Vugmeyster and Mangal 2020**, Characterizing exposure-response
  relationship for therapeutic monoclonal antibodies in immuno-oncology and
  beyond: challenges, perspectives, and prospects. *Clin Pharmacol Ther*
  108:1156–1170.
  [PMC7689749](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7689749/). Splits an
  apparent exposure-response relationship into exposure-driven,
  baseline-driven and response-driven parts, and reviews designs and analyses
  that separate them.
- ❌ **Sanghavi et al. 2024**, Covariate modeling in pharmacometrics: general
  points for consideration. *CPT: PSP* 13:710–728.
  [PMC11098153](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098153). The ISoP
  Standards & Best Practices Committee; states that a covariate-parameter
  association does not by itself imply a causal relationship.
- ❌ **Hernán and Robins**, *Causal Inference: What If* (2020), and their
  target trial emulation paper (*Am J Epidemiol* 2016). From epidemiology.
  *Citation not confirmed.*

**Gap.** The tools exist and are not a step in any PMX plan. The
specification's proposal stands: every validation plan carries a causal
diagram or a sentence saying why the question needs none.

## 4. Assay

**Asks.** Does the assay measure what the model assumes it measures, such as
free or total drug, active or total target, and is it accurate and precise
enough across the range the analysis uses? How are values below the limit of
quantification (BLQ) and anti-drug antibodies handled?

**Drug concentration assays.**

- ❌ **ICH M10**, Bioanalytical method validation and study sample analysis
  (Step 4 May 2022; FDA copy updated January 2025).
  [FDA copy](https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/sites/default/files/hhs-guidance-documents/FDA/50093493fnl_M10-Bioanalytical-Method-Validation-and-Study-Sample-Analysis_Jan-2025-update.pdf).
  Chromatographic methods and ligand binding assays; excludes biomarkers and
  immunogenicity. Replaced the 2011 EMA bioanalytical guideline.
- ❌ **Beal 2001**, Ways to fit a PK model with some data below the
  quantification limit. *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* 28:481–504.
  [doi:10.1023/A:1012299115260](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1012299115260).
  The M1 to M7 methods; discarding or substituting BLQ values biases the fit,
  and M3 treats them as censored.
- ❌ **Ahn et al. 2008**, Likelihood based approaches to handling data below
  the quantification limit using NONMEM VI. *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn*.
  *Citation not confirmed.*

**Biomarker assays.**

- ❌ **FDA guidance, January 2025**, Bioanalytical method validation for
  biomarkers. [PDF](https://fda.gov/media/185276/download). Under three pages;
  points to M10 as the starting point and asks for a fit-for-purpose
  approach scaled to the context of use.
- ❌ **Lee et al. 2006**, Fit-for-purpose method development and validation
  for successful biomarker measurement. *Pharm Res* 23:312–328.
  [doi:10.1007/s11095-005-9045-3](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11095-005-9045-3).
  The founding paper for validating a biomarker assay to the rigor its use
  needs.
- ❌ **CLSI H62**, Validation of assays performed by flow cytometry (2021).
  Relevant for cell counts such as B cells and T cells. *Citation not
  confirmed.*

**Immunogenicity assays.**

- ❌ **FDA guidance, February 2019**, Immunogenicity testing of therapeutic
  protein products: developing and validating assays for anti-drug antibody
  detection.
  [FDA page](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/immunogenicity-testing-therapeutic-protein-products-developing-and-validating-assays-anti-drug).
  Screening, confirmatory, titer and neutralizing assays; drug tolerance,
  which decides whether a patient with high drug levels can test ADA-positive
  at all.
- ❌ **Shankar et al. 2008**, recommendations for the validation of
  immunoassays used for detection of host antibodies against biotechnology
  products. *J Pharm Biomed Anal*. *Citation not confirmed.*

**Gap.** The assay literature validates the measurement for the laboratory.
None of it is written for a modeler checking that the measured quantity is
the one in the model: free against total drug for a target-mediated drug
disposition model, or whether an ADA assay's drug tolerance hides the
patients whose clearance the model attributes to antibodies.

## 5. Analysis Dataset

**Asks.** Is the analysis dataset built from the right files and versions,
are doses, times, missing values and BLQ values handled as intended, and do
derived variables and exclusions match the plan?

- ❌ **Bonate et al. 2012**, Guidelines for the quality control of population
  pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic analyses: an industry perspective. *AAPS J*
  14:749–758.
  [PMC3475847](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3475847). Data
  preparation, control streams, output, post-processing and report review;
  notes that published papers rarely state any quality assurance.
- ❌ **CDISC ADaM Population PK Implementation Guide (ADPPK) v1.0** (2023).
  The standard structure for a population PK analysis dataset, with time
  variables defined. Needs a free CDISC account.
  [ISoP standards page](https://www.isop.org/resources/standards).
- ❌ **ISoP PMx Data Programming Special Interest Group.**
  [Page](https://www.isop.org/special-interest-groups/pmxsig).
- ❌ **Cognigen posters on data assembly** (PAGE and ACoP, 2008 to 2010),
  which found dose records the most common source of dataset errors and built
  specification forms from that.
  [2009 poster](https://www.simulations-plus.com/wp-content/uploads/201_poster81_page_poster_2009jun10.pdf) ·
  [2010 forensic checks poster](https://www.simulations-plus.com/assets/213_poster92_PAGE_forensic_pmetrics_part1_2010jun08.pdf).
- ❌ [NMdata](https://cran.r-project.org/package=NMdata), an R package that
  checks a NONMEM dataset for consistency and traceability.
- ❌ [admiral](https://pharmaverse.github.io/admiral/), the pharmaverse
  package for building ADaM datasets, including the PK templates.
- ❌ The [Validation Checklist](../../references/Validation_Checklist.pdf),
  sections on importing and modifying data, and [xGx](http://opensource.nibr.com/xgx)
  exploratory graphics, which show the data before any model sees it.

**Gap.** Confirmed by the search. Bonate et al. and a set of posters are the
PMX literature on checking a dataset. No published checklist checks an
assembled dataset against its specification: dose records, event types, time
since first dose, covariate merges.

## 6. Sources and Prior Knowledge

**Asks.** Does each claim drawn from a paper, a label or a regulatory review
say what the source says, and is each prior or fixed parameter value traced
to where it came from?

- ❌ The status markers on this site's `references.qmd` pages, shaped as in
  [the TCE-IPDE references](../tce-ipde/references.qmd), and the
  [Reading Papers](../../guides/reading-papers.qmd) guide.
- ❌ The [Uncertainty Assessment Pedigree Table](../../references/Uncertainty_Assessment_Pedigree_Table.pdf),
  which grades each model input by the evidence behind it.
- ❌ **PRISMA 2020**, the reporting guideline for systematic reviews (Page et
  al., *BMJ* 2021), for a literature search that feeds a model-based
  meta-analysis. *Citation not confirmed.*

**Gap.** No PMX procedure for checking an agent's summary of a paper, or for
tracing every fixed parameter in a QSP model to its source.

## 7. Code

**Asks.** Do the model code, the data-handling scripts, the plotting code and
the simulation code compute what they claim to, and does the code run cleanly
from the start?

**Pharmacometrics.**

- ❌ Validation Checklist for R code:
  [PDF](../../references/Validation_Checklist.pdf) ·
  [Google Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rXf7mfFpjg1EWafuMaT_Dw29pa-onqr--n2LRULrS1Q/edit),
  written with Oliver Sander. Its planning section chooses the depth of review
  from the risk: unit tests, spot checks, code review, rerunning step by
  step, or independent reproduction.
- ❌ R Coding Checklist:
  [PDF](../../files/r-coding-checklist.pdf) ·
  [Google Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/17ec8YaARWZ6wppv3AfZCdaHfPwvOFUABXyXmENgHnpE/edit).
- ❌ Bonate et al. 2012 (under 5), for control streams and output listings.
- ❌ **Keizer, Karlsson and Hooker 2013**, Modeling and simulation workbench
  for NONMEM: tutorial on Pirana, PsN, and Xpose. *CPT: PSP*. *Citation not
  confirmed.*
- ❌ **R Validation Hub**, A risk-based approach for assessing R package
  accuracy within a validated infrastructure (white paper), and the
  [riskmetric](https://pharmaverse.github.io/riskmetric/) package that came
  from it. For whether the packages an analysis depends on can be trusted.
  The white paper's author list differs between sources.
- ❌ **PHUSE Good Programming Practice guidance**, and the practice of
  independent double programming from clinical statistical programming:
  a second programmer reproduces each output from the specification, and the
  two are compared. Industry papers now argue for scaling it to risk.
  [PHUSE GPP](https://advance.phuse.global/x/IAMF).

**Code written by AI.**

- ❌ A 2024 *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* study of ChatGPT and Gemini writing
  NONMEM control streams: structural and syntax errors, and output that was
  not reproducible between runs.
  [doi:10.1007/s10928-024-09921-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10928-024-09921-y).
- ❌ **PKGPT** (*Pharmaceutics* 18:501, 2026), an agent that runs NONMEM and
  revises the control stream. Models converged on three public datasets but
  missed established covariates and gave an implausible peripheral volume.
  [MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4923/18/4/501).
- ❌ A 2026 medRxiv preprint on language-model-generated propofol PK
  simulation code: accurate in most runs, silently wrong in a minority, and
  so needing validation against a reference implementation.
  [medRxiv](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.04.27.26351582v1.full.pdf).
- ❌ [Validating Code Written by an AI Agent](agent-written-code.qmd), this
  project's own document.

**Gap.** Every PMX source assumes a person wrote the code and a second person
reviews it. The three AI studies measure failure rates; none proposes a
review procedure.

## 8. Model

**Asks.** Does the model describe the data, and are its parameters plausible?
What counts as evidence depends on the kind of model, so the sources are
grouped by kind.

**Population PK and PK/PD models.**

- ❌ **FDA guidance, February 2022**, Population pharmacokinetics.
  [FDA page](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/population-pharmacokinetics).
  Model evaluation and the content of a population PK report.
- ❌ **EMA guideline, 2007**, Reporting the results of population
  pharmacokinetic analyses.
  [EMA page](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/reporting-results-population-pharmacokinetic-analyses).
- ❌ **Nguyen et al. 2017**, Model evaluation of continuous data
  pharmacometric models: metrics and graphics. *CPT: PSP* 6:87–109.
  [PMC5321813](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5321813). The ISoP
  Model Evaluation Group's tutorial; each diagnostic shown for a correctly
  specified and a misspecified model.
- ❌ **Byon et al. 2013**, Establishing best practices and guidance in
  population modeling: an experience with an internal population
  pharmacokinetic analysis guidance. *CPT: PSP* 2:e51.
  [PMC6483270](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6483270). Pfizer's
  internal guidance and model-building workflow.
- ❌ **Karlsson and Savic 2007**, Diagnosing model diagnostics. *Clin
  Pharmacol Ther* 82:17–20. *Citation not confirmed.*
- ❌ Residual and simulation diagnostics, each the founding paper for its
  method. *Citations not confirmed.*
  - Conditional weighted residuals (CWRES): Hooker, Staatz and Karlsson 2007,
    *Pharm Res*.
  - Normalized prediction distribution errors (NPDE): Brendel et al. 2006,
    *Pharm Res*; the npde package, Comets et al. 2008.
  - Prediction-corrected visual predictive checks (pcVPC): Bergstrand et al.
    2011, *AAPS J*.
  - Posterior predictive checks: Yano, Beal and Sheiner 2001, *J
    Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn*.
  - Shrinkage, and when individual estimates mislead diagnostics: Savic and
    Karlsson 2009, *AAPS J*.
- ❌ **Sanghavi et al. 2024** (under 3), and **Hutmacher and Kowalski
  2015**, Covariate selection in pharmacometric analyses: a review of
  methods. *Br J Clin Pharmacol* 79:132–147.
  [PMC4294083](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4294083). The
  problems with stepwise selection; Ribbing and Jonsson 2004 (*J
  Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn*) on selection bias in covariate effects
  (*citation not confirmed*).
- ❌ Tools: [ggPMX](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggPMX),
  [xgxr](https://cran.r-project.org/package=xgxr), PsN and Xpose, and
  [See-Value](https://www.see-value.com) for lineups, which hide the real
  data's plot among plots simulated from the model.

**Exposure-response models.**

- ❌ **Overgaard, Ingwersen and Tornøe 2015**, Establishing good practices for
  exposure-response analysis of clinical endpoints in drug development. *CPT:
  PSP* 4:565–575.
  [PMC4625861](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4625861). Planning,
  conducting and showing an exposure-response analysis, tied to the question
  each step answers.
- ❌ FDA 2003 exposure-response guidance (under 2), and Dai et al. 2020
  (under 3).

**Quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) models.**

- ❌ **Gadkar et al. 2016**, A six-stage workflow for robust application of
  systems pharmacology. *CPT: PSP* 5:235–249.
  [PMC4879472](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4879472). Needs and
  goals, scope, biology, behaviors, knowledge gaps and variability, design.
- ❌ **Friedrich 2016**, A model qualification method for mechanistic
  physiological QSP models to support model-informed drug development. *CPT:
  PSP* 5:43–53.
  [PMC4761232](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4761232). Argues that
  the validation used for PK/PD models does not fit QSP models, and covers
  scope, uncertainty, variability and comparison to data.
- ❌ **Cucurull-Sanchez et al. 2019**, Best practices to maximize the use and
  reuse of quantitative and systems pharmacology models: recommendations from
  the United Kingdom quantitative and systems pharmacology network. *CPT: PSP*
  8:259–272. [PMC6533407](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6533407/).
- ❌ **Braakman, Pathmanathan and Moore 2022**, Evaluation framework for
  systems models. *CPT: PSP* 11:264–289.
  [PMC8923730](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8923730).
  Sensitivity, identifiability, validation and uncertainty quantification,
  with examples of the misleading results a poor choice of analysis gives.
- ❌ **Sher et al. 2022**, A quantitative systems pharmacology perspective on
  the importance of parameter identifiability. *Bull Math Biol* 84:39.
  [PMC8821410](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8821410).
- ❌ **Stein and Looby 2018**, Benchmarking QSP models against simple models:
  a path to improved comprehension and predictive performance. *CPT: PSP*
  7:487–489. [doi:10.1002/psp4.12311](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12311).
- ❌ **Stein, Kearns, Kim and Margolskee 2021**,
  [Cheat sheet for model uncertainty assessment](https://zenodo.org/records/4409236),
  version 1.2, Zenodo. Written with QSP models in mind; used at scoping and
  again at the end of an activity.
- ❌ Musuamba et al. 2021 (under the credibility frameworks).

**Physiologically based PK (PBPK) models.**

- ❌ **Shebley et al. 2018**, Physiologically based pharmacokinetic model
  qualification and reporting procedures for regulatory submissions: a
  consortium perspective. *Clin Pharmacol Ther* 104:88–110.
  [PMC6032820](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6032820). Qualifying
  the platform and the model, from the Simcyp Consortium.
- ❌ **EMA guideline**, Reporting of physiologically based pharmacokinetic
  (PBPK) modelling and simulation (2018).
  [EMA page](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/qualification-reporting-physiologically-based-pharmacokinetic-pbpk-modelling-simulation).
  Covers platform qualification as well as reporting.
- ❌ **FDA guidance, 2018**, Physiologically based pharmacokinetic analyses:
  format and content. *Citation not confirmed.*
- ❌ Kuemmel et al. 2020 (under the credibility frameworks).

**Machine learning models.** See TRIPOD+AI and PROBAST under Other Fields.
No PMX-specific evaluation standard was found.

**Gap.** No written model evaluation checklist for population models; Nguyen
et al. is the nearest, and it is a tutorial on plots. Plausibility against
physiology and against published values is in every guideline's prose and in
no checklist. The QSP literature has four frameworks and no agreement among
them.

## 9. Predictions

**Asks.** Is the uncertainty in a prediction stated, including the
uncertainty from assumptions and not only from parameter estimates? Is the
prediction inside the range the data support? Does the model predict better
than a simple one would?

- ❌ [Cheat sheet for model uncertainty assessment](https://zenodo.org/records/4409236)
  (under 8), with the
  [Uncertainty Assessment Pedigree Table](../../references/Uncertainty_Assessment_Pedigree_Table.pdf)
  and the
  [Presentation on Managing Uncertainty](../../references/Uncertainty_Assessment_Presentation.pdf).
- ❌ Stein and Looby 2018 (under 8), on benchmarking against a simple model.
- ❌ **Dosne, Bergstrand, Harling and Karlsson 2016**, Improving the
  estimation of parameter uncertainty distributions in nonlinear mixed
  effects models using sampling importance resampling. *J Pharmacokinet
  Pharmacodyn* 43:583–596.
  [PMC5110709](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5110709/). Parameter
  uncertainty where the covariance matrix and the bootstrap fail: small
  datasets and nonlinear models.
- ❌ **Holford et al. 1999**, Simulation in drug development: good practices,
  a report from the Center for Drug Development Science. Cited widely; the
  original web page may no longer resolve. *Citation not confirmed.*
- ❌ **Gneiting and Raftery 2007**, Strictly proper scoring rules,
  prediction, and estimation. *J Am Stat Assoc*. From statistics: how to
  score a probabilistic prediction against what happened. *Citation not
  confirmed.*

**Gap.** Stein and Looby argue for benchmarking and do not give a procedure:
which simple model, which held-out data, what difference in predictive
performance counts. No PMX source covers checking an extrapolation to doses,
populations or durations outside the data.

## 10. Conclusions

**Asks.** Does the conclusion follow from the result? A model can be right
and the claim drawn from it wrong, most often a causal claim from
observational exposure-response data, or a covariate effect read as a
mechanism.

- ❌ The causal sources under 3, used now to check the final claims against
  the diagram drawn at the start.
- ❌ Sanghavi et al. 2024 (under 3), on interpreting covariate effects.
- ❌ ICH E9(R1) (under 2): a conclusion has to be about the estimand the study
  was designed for.

**Gap.** Multiple comparisons and selective reporting across models tried are
not covered by any PMX source found.

## 11. Communication

**Asks.** Do the figures, slides and report show what the analysis found,
with its uncertainty, and without overstating it?

- ❌ [Graphics Principles Cheat Sheet](../../references/Graphics_Principles_Cheat_Sheet_v1.1.pdf)
  and the
  [Effective Visual Communication tutorial](https://ascpt.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/psp4.12455)
  (*CPT: PSP*).
- ❌ [Presentation Checklist](../../references/Presentation_Checklist_v2.03.pdf)
  and the Presentation Evaluation Feedback Form:
  [PDF](../../files/presentation-evaluation-form.pdf) ·
  [Google Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1K_lcsG6sClLQcd5sm_ezcvtD9ccmm0uM/edit).
- ❌ **Dykstra et al. 2015**, Reporting guidelines for population
  pharmacokinetic analyses. *J Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn* 42:301–314.
  [PMC4432104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4432104/). Also
  published in *J Clin Pharmacol*. Industry, consulting and FDA authors; the
  report's two jobs are stating the findings and their effect on decisions,
  and documenting the methods well enough for review and reuse.
- ❌ EMA 2007 population PK reporting guideline and Marshall et al. 2016
  (documentation), above.

**Gap.** Reporting guidance exists for population PK. Nothing checks whether a
slide or a summary overstates what the analysis found, which is the step an
AI-written summary is most likely to get wrong.

## 12. Reproducibility

**Asks.** Can someone else rerun the analysis from its inputs and get the same
numbers, and is there a record of what was checked and by whom?

- ❌ The [Validation Checklist](../../references/Validation_Checklist.pdf),
  overall section.
- ❌ Cucurull-Sanchez et al. 2019 (under 8), on model reuse.
- ❌ **Sandve et al. 2013**, Ten simple rules for reproducible computational
  research. *PLoS Comput Biol*. *Citation not confirmed.*
- ❌ **Wilkinson et al. 2016**, The FAIR guiding principles for scientific
  data management and stewardship. *Sci Data*. *Citation not confirmed.*

**Gap.** When an agent did the work, the prompts and the session may belong
in the record. No source addresses that.

## 13. Use

**Asks.** Was the answer used for the decision it was meant to inform, and
did the decision turn out the way the analysis said it would?

- ❌ ICH M15's "model impact" element (above), which asks the question
  prospectively.
- ❌ The Marshall et al. 2019 follow-up to the MID3 paper, on how practice
  matches the standard.

**Gap.** No practice of following an analysis to its decision and back. The
[PMX internship specification](../pmx-internship/specification.qmd) checks
use three months after an internship, for one project.

## Software Engineering

Covered for ideas, not exhaustively. Each line is a practice PMX could borrow.

- **Verification and validation as a discipline.** IEEE 1012, the standard
  for system, software and hardware verification and validation; Oberkampf
  and Roy, *Verification and Validation in Scientific Computing* (Cambridge,
  2010), which separates code verification, solution verification and
  validation against experiment. *Citations not confirmed.*
- **Testing.** Unit tests for each function, regression tests that compare
  output with a stored reference, and property-based tests that check a rule
  holds over many generated inputs (concentrations never negative, mass
  balanced). The propofol preprint above is an argument for reference tests.
- **Code review.** A second person reads every change before it is merged,
  as in the [Google engineering practices](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/)
  guide. The PMX equivalent is the reviewer in the Validation Checklist.
- **Independent reimplementation.** Double programming, above, and N-version
  programming in safety-critical software: two teams build the same thing and
  the outputs are compared.
- **Continuous integration.** Every change runs the tests automatically, so a
  broken check is found when it breaks.
- **Pinned environments.** `renv`, containers and lock files, so a rerun uses
  the same package versions. This site's frozen computation does the same job
  for its pages.
- **Good practice papers for scientists.** Wilson et al. 2014, Best practices
  for scientific computing (*PLoS Biol*), and Wilson et al. 2017, Good enough
  practices in scientific computing (*PLoS Comput Biol*). *Citations not
  confirmed.*

## Other Fields

Frameworks from fields that validate models for decisions, each with what PMX
could take from it.

- **Medical devices.** ❌ ASME V&V 40-2018 (above), and ❌ the FDA guidance
  Assessing the credibility of computational modeling and simulation in
  medical device submissions (2023, *citation not confirmed*). The most
  developed risk-based credibility framework; the drug frameworks are
  adaptations of it.
- **Health economics.** ❌ **Eddy et al. 2012**, Model transparency and
  validation: a report of the ISPOR-SMDM Modeling Good Research Practices Task
  Force-7. *Value Health* 15:843–850, also in *Med Decis Making*.
  [ISPOR page](https://www.ispor.org/heor-resources/good-practices/article/model-transparency-and-validation).
  Five kinds of validation: face validity, verification, cross validity,
  external validity and predictive validity, the last two the strongest. A
  ready-made taxonomy for kinds 7 to 9 here.
- **Clinical prediction models.** ❌ **TRIPOD+AI** (Collins et al., *BMJ*
  2024), the reporting guideline for prediction models including machine
  learning, and ❌ **PROBAST** (Wolff et al., *Ann Intern Med* 2019), a tool
  for judging the risk of bias in a prediction model study. The nearest
  standards for an ML model in PMX. *Citations not confirmed.*
- **Bayesian statistics.** ❌ **Gelman et al. 2020**, Bayesian workflow
  (arXiv), and ❌ **Talts et al. 2018**, Validating Bayesian inference
  algorithms with simulation-based calibration (arXiv). Prior predictive
  checks, fake-data simulation to check that a fit recovers known parameters,
  and posterior predictive checks. Fitting simulated data with known
  parameters is a check for kind 7 that PMX rarely runs. *Citations not
  confirmed.*
- **Machine learning documentation.** ❌ Model cards (Mitchell et al. 2019)
  and ❌ datasheets for datasets (Gebru et al. 2021): a standard one-page
  record of what a model or dataset is for and where it fails. A model card
  for a PMX model would be a short form of the Context of Use table plus the
  validation plan. *Citations not confirmed.*
- **Epidemiology.** Target trial emulation (under 3).
- **Systematic reviews.** PRISMA 2020 (under 6).

## Gaps Found

The [specification's ranked gaps](specification.qmd#gaps-ranked) are built
from this list. The search confirmed the specification's earlier gaps and added
three.

1. **Dataset assembly checklist** (5). Confirmed: one paper and some posters.
2. **Model evaluation checklist** (8). Confirmed: a tutorial on plots, and
   guideline prose.
3. **Study fitness for the model** (2). New. Nothing asks whether an existing
   study can support the model about to be fitted.
4. **Assay fitness for the model** (4). New. Assays are validated for the
   laboratory, not for whether they measure the model's quantity.
5. **A causal diagram as a standing step** (3). The tools exist and no plan
   asks for them.
6. **A benchmarking procedure** (9).
7. **Reviewing AI-written work** (7, 11). New in scope. Three studies measure
   how often AI-written PMX code fails; the FDA AI draft covers AI models
   that produce evidence; nothing covers an AI doing the analyst's work.
8. **Checking claims against sources** (6), as a portable tool.

## What Was Searched and Not Found

- A revision of the 2003 FDA exposure-response guidance.
- A final version of the January 2025 FDA AI draft guidance.
- A second ISoP Model Evaluation Group tutorial, for discrete data.
- Upreti and Venkatakrishnan's model-based meta-analysis (MBMA) paper (2019),
  which was expected to cover MBMA good practice. MBMA has no section here
  until a source is found.
